Thus, the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals’ holding that the Western Washington Growth Management Hearings Board had jurisdiction to review whether Thurston County’s urban growth areas violate the Growth Management Act and whether Thurston County’s comprehensive plan provides for a variety of rural densities. However, the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals’ holding that a county must identify and justify the use of a land market supply factor in making its urban growth area designations and its holding that densities greater than one dwelling unit per five acres cannot be included in the rural component of a comprehensive plan and remanded the case to the Western Washington Growth Management Hearings Board to consider whether Thurston County’s urban growth area designations were clearly erroneous in light of local circumstances and whether the various densities included by Thurston County in the rural component of its comprehensive plan and its use of innovative zoning techniques provide for a variety of rural densitites.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Tukwila v. Garrett
facts: Respondent Kellas Garrett was convicted of violating a temporary protection order in the Tukwila Municipal Court and sentenced. Garrett subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that the jury pool from which the jury was drawn had been improperly selected in violation of Washington Revised Code §2.36.050 insofar as the jury pool, having been comprised of residents of three zip codes that contain but are not limited to the city of Tukwila, had included individuals residing outside of Tukwila and insofar as none of the jurors actually selected were residents of Tukwila. The Superior Court for King County vacated Garrett’s conviction, ruling that there had been a material departure from §2.36.050’s requirements for jury selection given that the Tukwila Municipal Court has no authority to summon jurors from outside of Tukwila. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §2.36.050 require that juries empaneled by the Tukwila Municipal Court be comprised entirely of residents of Tukwila?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court reversed the Superior Court for King County and reinstated Garrett’s conviction, concluding that although §2.36.050 requires that jurors be selected from the population of the area served by the court, statutory requirements relating to jury pools are merely directory and need only be substantially complied with so long as a fair and impartial jury is selected. Thus, as the three zip codes from which jurors were drawn roughly encompass the city of Tukwila and as there was no indication that the jury had not been fair and impartial or that Garrett had suffered any actual prejudice as a result of the selection procedure, the Court held that §2.36.050 had been substantially complied with.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Puapuaga
facts: Jesie Puapuaga was charged with second degree murder in the Superior Court for Pierce County and ordered to undergo a competency evaluation at Western State Hospital. Upon Puapuaga’s arrival, an inventory of his property revealed a box appearing to contain autopsy photos of the victim and a threatening note directed to one of Puapuaga’s co-defendants, which the state of Washington impounded. The trial court subsequently ordered a special master to review the impounded materials in the presence of defense counsel, determine whether they contain any privileged communications and redact them appropriately if so, and turn the materials over to the trial court for the trial court to determine what materials, if any, should be turned over to the state. Puapuaga appealed the trial court’s order, asserting that the state had seized his personal property in violation of the 4th Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I §7 of the Washington State Constitution and thereby violated the rules of discovery in a manner that prejudiced him in his ability to prepare for trial and necessitates dismissal of the charge against him.
questions: Did the state unlawfully seize Puapuaga’s personal property? Did the seizure prejudice Puapuaga in his ability to prepare for trial?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the trial court’s order, concluding that the seizure of Puapuaga’s personal property was not in violation of Puapuaga’s constitutional right to privacy insofar as Puapuaga had a significantly lowered expectation of privacy when he was admitted to Western State Hospital for court ordered evaluation. The Court also held that it could not determine whether the seizure prejudiced Puapuaga in his ability to prepare for trial given the lack of a clear nexus between the contents of the box and the charge against Puapuaga and that the disposition of the box should be therefore determined by the special master and the trial court.

title: University of Washington Medical Center v. Department of Health
facts: As required by Washington Revised Code §70.38, Swedish Medical Center applied for a certificate of need in anticipation of establishing a liver transplant program. Pursuant to §70.38’s public comment provisions, the respondent University of Washington Medical Center subsequently objected to the application and requested a public hearing. After considering the evidence presented by both Swedish Medical Center and the University of Washington Medical Center, the petitioner Department of Health granted Swedish Medical Center the certificate of need. The University of Washington Medical Center appealed the decision to a health law judge, who affirmed the Department of Health’s decision after restricting the new evidence that could be presented to evidence directly relevant to the record that the decision was based upon. The University of Washington Medical Center sought judicial review in the Superior Court for Thurston County, which reversed the health law judge’s limitation of the scope of admissible evidence to evidence that existed at the time the public comment period closed and vacated the decision to grant Swedish Medical Center a certificate of need. The Department of Health appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the health law judge abuse their discretion by restricting the scope of admissible evidence to evidence that existed at the time the public comment period closed? If not, did substantial evidence support the Department of Health’s decision to grant Swedish Medical Center a certificate of need? Was Swedish Medical Center’s application for a certificate of need fatally flawed by its failure to consider the impact of establishing a second liver transplant program in the state of Washington upon the University of Washington Medical Center’s training program?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Superior Court for Thurston County, concluding that the health law judge did not abuse their discretion by restricting the scope of admissible evidence to evidence that existed at the time the public comment period closed given that §70.38 and its associated administrative regulations clearly contemplate that final decisions regarding certificates of need will be made expeditiously within 90 days of an application being submitted. Thus, as the Court also held that substantial evidence supported the Department of Health’s decision to grant Swedish Medical Center a certificate of need and that Swedish Medical Center’s application for a certificate of need was not fatally flawed insofar as applicants are not required to evaluate the impact of a program upon a potential competitor, the Court reinstated the certificate of need.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Ranger Insurance Company v. Pierce County
facts: Signature Bail Bonds issued a number of bail bonds in Pierce County on behalf of respondent Ranger Insurance Company as well as on behalf of Granite State Insurance Company that were forfeited when defendants failed to appear in court. After Signature Bail Bonds used funds provided by Ranger Insurance Company to cover not only the forfeited bonds issued in Ranger Insurance Company’s name but also those issued in Granite State Insurance Company’s name and subsequently failed to forward bond money returned to it by Pierce County when the defendants were apprehended, Ranger Insurance Company charged Pierce County with negligently handling its funds and filed suit against it. The trial court granted summary judgment for Pierce County, ruling that the county had observed the requisite standard of care. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that there was no record of Ranger Insurance Company making any objective manifestations supporting Signature Bail Bonds’ apparent authority to divert its funds to satisfy obligations belonging to other sureties. Pierce County appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is there a genuine issue of material fact as to whether Pierce County observed the requisite standard of care in allowing Signature Bail Bonds to divert Ranger Insurance Company’s funds to satisfy obligations belonging to other sureties?
conclusions: Justice Sanders’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that a genuine issue of material fact exists insofar as a reasonable jury could find that Pierce County failed to act as a reasonably prudent clerk in receiving, allocating, and disbursing funds insofar as the only objective manifestations made by Ranger Insurance Company with regard to Signature Bail Bonds' authority to act on its behalf were limited to bonds issued in Ranger Insurance Company’s name. Thus, the Court remanded the case to the trial court.

title: Costanich v. Department of Social and Health Services
facts: After the respondent Department of Social and Health Services revoked petitioner Kathie Costanich’s foster care license, Costanich sought review of the Department of Health and Social Services’ decision in the Superior Court for King County. The superior court reversed the Department of Social and Health Services’ decision and awarded Costanich $25,000 in attorney’s fees, the maximum amount authorized by Washington Revised Code §4.84.350, which grants reasonable attorney’s fees to prevailing parties in cases reviewing the actions of state agencies. Upon appeal, the superior court’s decision was affirmed and Costanich was awarded additional attorney’s fees for costs incurred in the appellate process. The Department of Social and Health Services subsequently filed a motion to amend the order, asserting that §4.84.350 limits the total amount of attorney’s fees awarded to prevailing parties to $25,000. The Washington Court of Appeals granted the motion. Costanich appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §4.84.350’s $25,000 limit on attorney’s fees apply to each level of judicial review or to all levels of judicial review combined? Did the Department of Social and Health Services waive its right to appeal the award of attorney’s fees by failing to timely object?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although the Department of Social and Health Services had not waived its right to appeal the award of attorney’s fees insofar as no court may award attorney’s fees in excess of the amount authorized by statute, §4.84.350 does permit Costanich to collect up to $25,000 in attorney’s fees at each level of judicial review, including the Court’s review of the Washington Court of Appeals.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Quismundo
facts: Petitioner Ronald Quismundo was convicted of violating a no contact order in the Superior Court for Snohomish County after a trial in which Quismundo unsuccessfully moved for dismissal of the charge with prejudice on grounds that the charging document erroneously failed to allege that he violated the no contact order. Quismundo subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that the trial court erred in permitting the respondent state of Washington to amend the charging document. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Quismundo’s conviction, holding that the trial court properly rejected Quismundo’s motion insofar as it requested an improper remedy. Quismundo appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the trial court err in permitting the state to amend the insufficient charging document rather than dismissing the charge?
conclusions: Justice Stephens’ opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and remanded the case to the trial court for dismissal of the charge, concluding that the proper remedy for an insufficient charging document is dismissal of the charge without prejudice and that the trial court should therefore have responded to Quismundo’s motion by dismissing the charge without prejudice regardless of the fact that Quismundo’s requested remedy of dismissal with prejudice would have been improper and regardless of whether Quismundo was prejudiced by the insufficiency.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Schonder v. Lundeberg
questions: Whether a trial court properly excluded evidence of a liability release form allegedly signed by a cosmetic tattoo client.

title: State of Washington v. Alvarado
facts: Petitioner Alexander Alvarado was convicted of two counts of burglary, one count of first degree theft, two counts of first degree possession of stolen property, and one count of second degree possession of stolen property in the Superior Court for Whatcom County. The trial court subsequently imposed an exceptional sentence upon Alvarado on grounds that imposing a sentence within the standard range would have resulted in Alvarado receiving no time in prison for four of his convictions as multiple current offenses due to the fact that his numerous prior convictions gave him such a high offender score that the additional current convictions would not increase his standard sentence range beyond the standard sentence range he already faced simply for the first count of burglary. Alvarado appealed his sentence to the Washington Court of Appeals, which certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the trial court properly apply the provisions of Washington Revised Code §9.94A.535 that permit courts to impose exceptional sentences in cases in which a high offender score results in some current offenses going unpunished? Was the imposition of an exceptional sentence upon Alvarado consistent with the United States Supreme Court’s holding in Blakely v. Washington that the 6th Amendment to the United States Constitution requires determinations regarding the appropriateness of exceptional sentences to be made by the jury?
conclusions: Justice Stephens’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the imposition of an exceptional sentence upon Alvarado was consistent with §9.94A.535 insofar as language in §9.94A.535 referring to current offenses going unpunished was clearly intended to authorize the imposition of exceptional sentences in cases such as Alvarado’s in which a defendant receives no time in prison for some current offenses as a result of a high offender score. The Court also held that the imposition of an exceptional sentence upon Alvarado was consistent with Blakely v. Washington as the trial court’s determination that some current offenses would go unpunished if an exceptional sentence was not imposed did not involve fact finding reserved for the jury but rather simply involved reference to Alvarado’s criminal history and calculation of his offender score.

title: State of Washington v. Xiong
facts: Petitioner Bee Xiong was charged with possession of methamphetamine with intent to deliver in the Superior Court for Spokane County after he was mistakenly detained by police officers attempting to serve an arrest warrant on his brother and a subsequent search of his person revealed methamphetamine and other drug paraphernalia. The trial court granted Xiong’s motion to suppress the evidence derived from the search, ruling that the warrantless search was not justified by a reasonable belief that Xiong was armed and presently dangerous and therefore in violation of the 4th Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article II §7 of the Washington State Constitution. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed the trial court’s suppression order, holding that the search was justified by officer safety concerns. Xiong appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was the search of Xiong’s person justified by a reasonable belief that Xiong was armed and presently dangerous?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and reinstated the trial court’s suppression order, concluding that as Xiong was handcuffed, made no attempt to flee or to reach into his pockets, and was cooperative, there were no exigent circumstances suggesting a threat to officer safety that would justify a search.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Jensen
facts: Petitioner William Jensen was convicted of four counts of solicitation to commit murder in the Superior Court for King County after soliciting a fellow inmate and an undercover police officer to murder four members of his family while he was jailed for threatening his wife. Jensen subsequently appealed three of his convictions, asserting that the unit of prosecution under Washington Revised Code §9A.28.030(1) is the enticement to commit a crime rather than the number of potential victims. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Jensen’s convictions. Jensen appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is the unit of prosecution under §9A.28.030(1) the enticement to commit a crime or the number of potential victims?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, vacated two of Jensen’s convictions, and remanded the case to the trial court for resentencing, concluding that a single enticement to commit multiple crimes is a single solicitation for purposes of §9A.28.030(1). Thus, as Jensen had initially enticed a fellow inmate to murder three members of his family and subsequently enticed an undercover police officer purporting to represent the fellow inmate to expand the agreement to include his son as well, the Court held that Jensen had committed two solicitations.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Potter vs. Washington State Patrol
facts: After petitioner Mark Potter was cited for driving with a suspended driver’s license, his automobile was impounded and eventually auctioned by the respondent Washington State Patrol pursuant to the procedures outlined in Washington Administrative Code §204-96-010. Asserting that his automobile had been unlawfully converted, Potter filed a class action suit against the Washington State Patrol on behalf of himself and all of the owners of automobiles impounded pursuant to §204-96-010. The trial court granted the Washington State Patrol’s motion for summary judgment, ruling that the Washington State Patrol’s exercise of authority in impounding and auctioning Potter’s automobile was privileged and that it therefore could not be held liable for conversion. Upon appeal, the Supreme Court of Washington reversed, holding that the Washington State Patrol’s exercise of its authority was not privileged. The Washington State Patrol moved for reconsideration to review whether Washington Revised Code §46.55 bars Potter’s action. The Court granted the motion.
questions: Are the procedures for appealing impoundments outlined in §46.55 the exclusive remedy for unlawful impoundments?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court concluded that §46.55 does not abrogate common law claims of conversion and therefore does not bar Potter’s action insofar as §46.55 does not contain any explicit language declaring itself the exclusive remedy for unlawful impoundments and does not otherwise indicate that the legislature intended for it to be an exclusive remedy. Thus, the Court remanded the case to the trial court.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Mutual  of Enumclaw Insurance Company v. T & G Construction, Inc.
facts: The Villas at Harbour Pointe Owners Association filed suit against petitioner T & G Construction, Inc. in the Superior Court for Snohomish County after siding that T & G Construction had installed was found to be defective. After T & G Construction reached a settlement with the Villas at Harbour Pointe Owners Association and the parties sought a reasonableness determination from the superior court, respondent Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company, T & G Construction’s insurer, appeared at the subsequent reasonableness hearing and objected to the settlement. Following the superior court’s approval of the settlement, Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company petitioned the Superior Court for King County for a declaratory judgment that T & G Construction is not liable for the defective construction on grounds that the statute of limitations had expired, that the damages awarded to the Villas at Harbour Pointe Owners Association in the settlement were outside of the scope of the coverage provisions of T & G Construction’s insurance policy, and that T & G Construction had breached its obligation to cooperate with its insurer. The trial court granted summary judgment for T & G Construction. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company should be permitted to fully litigate the question of whether the statute of limitations had expired and that, if it were determined that the statute of limitations had not expired, the trial court should also consider whether Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company had been prejudiced by T & G Construction’s failure to cooperate with it during settlement negotiations. T & G Construction appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company entitled to fully litigate the question of whether T & Construction is not liable for the defective construction on grounds that the statute of limitations had expired? Were the damages awarded to Villas at Harbour Pointe Owners Association in the settlement outside of the scope of the coverage provisions of T & G Construction’s insurance policy? Did T & G Construction breach its obligation to cooperate with its insurer?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed in part and reversed in part the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that insurers are not entitled to relitigate questions that were resolved in the underlying case either by judgment or by arm’s length settlement and that Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company had not been prejudiced by any breach of T & G Construction’s obligation to cooperate with its insurer given that Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company refused to participate in settlement negotiations. However, the Court also held that the record was unclear regarding the applicability of coverage exceptions in T & G Construction’s insurance policy and therefore remanded the case to the trial court to consider whether these exceptions apply.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Miller v. Campbell
facts: Alleging that his late stepfather Patrick Campbell had sexually abused him over the course of several years during his childhood, respondent Michael Miller filed suit against Campbell’s estate in the Superior Court for Snohomish County. The estate subsequently filed a motion for summary judgment on grounds that Miller was estopped from pursuing the claim due to the fact that he had failed to list the claim as an asset during bankruptcy proceedings. The trial court granted summary judgment for the estate. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that Miller was not estopped from pursuing the claim insofar as victims of childhood sexual abuse are frequently not cognizant of the connection between the abuse and the resulting psychological harm for many years and that therefore Miller may have lacked knowledge of a potential tort claim at the time of his bankruptcy. The estate appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington. After Miller’s bankruptcy trustee reopened Miller’s bankruptcy case in response to the Washington Court of Appeals’ decision and determined that the bankruptcy estate owns Miller’s claim against Campbell’s estate, Miller filed a motion to substitute the bankruptcy trustee as the real party in interest in the case. The Court granted the motion.
questions: May the doctrine of judicial estoppel bar a bankruptcy trustee that has been substituted as the real party in interest from bringing a previously undisclosed claim on behalf of the bankruptcy estate?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for a unanimous Court concluded that the bankruptcy trustee was not barred from bringing a claim against Campbell’s estate on behalf of the bankruptcy estate by Miller’s failure to disclose the claim during his bankruptcy proceedings as the doctrine of judicial estoppel generally has no application against a debtor when a bankruptcy trustee has been substituted as the real party in interest. Thus, the Court remanded the case to the trial court.

title: State of Washington v. Griffith
facts: Petitioner Joan Griffith pled guilty to possessing stolen property in the second degree in the Superior Court for Spokane County after attempting to sell jewelry that had been stolen in a burglary. The trial court subsequently ordered Griffith to pay restitution in the amount of the value of the stolen jewelry that had not been recovered ($11,500). Griffith appealed the restitution order, asserting that there was insufficient evidence to support it insofar as she had merely pled guilty to possessing $250 to $1,500 worth of stolen property and there was no evidence indicating that she was in possession of all of the jewelry that had been stolen in the burglary. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the restitution order. Griffith appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was the trial court’s order that Griffith pay $11,500 in restitution supported by substantial evidence?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the evidence supporting the trial court’s restitution order was insufficient given that Griffith had not been convicted of the burglary and had been identified by eyewitnesses as being in possession of only one of the numerous items of stolen jewelry that remained unrecovered. Thus, the Court vacated the restitution order and remanded the case to the trial court for a new restitution hearing.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: In re disciplinary proceeding against Poole
facts: Disciplinary proceedings were held against petitioner attorney Jeffrey Poole for failing to provide timely or complete response to various requests for information and documents made by the Office of Disciplinary Counsel in previous disciplinary proceedings, violating Washington Rules of Professional Conduct §8.4 (c), (d), and (l). Poole was also charged for failing to maintain accurate accounts and failure to keep all client funds in the designated trust account. The Washington State Bar Association Disciplinary Board affirmed the hearing officer’s recommended sanction of a one-year suspension from practicing law, followed by a two-year probationary period. Poole challenged that the findings of fact were contradictory, and argued his failure to respond was inadvertent due to personal and emotional problems. The Supreme Court of Washington granted Poole’s petition for review.
questions: Was the hearing officer’s findings of fact contradictory, and did the hearing officer subsequently err in establishing the aggravating and mitigating factors based on the evidence in the record?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court held that the hearing officer’s findings of fact were not contradictory as Poole argued, but rather the evidence supported the findings that Poole’s failure to respond to the requests for the billing statements occurred one way or another, and there was no reason why the hearing officer needed to specifically determine how the events occurred. No matter how the event is viewed, Poole’s conduct resulted in the violation of Washington Rules of Professional Conduct §8.4 (c), (d), and (l), and Washington Enforcement Law Rules of Conduct §5.3(e) and §13.8. The hearing officer correctly established the aggravating and mitigating factors by giving little weight to Poole’s personal and emotional problems because they did merely impacted, but did not cause, the misconduct. Thus, affirming that Poole knowingly made the violations, the Court imposed the one-year suspension as recommended by the hearing officer and the Board, followed by a two-year probation.

title: State of Washington v. Neth
facts: Petitioner Joseph Neth was convicted of possession of methamphetamine with intent to deliver after a search of his automobile following a traffic stop revealed a large quantity of cash, methamphetamine, and drug paraphernalia. Neth subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that without a drug dog that had been brought to the scene alerting police officers that drugs were present in the automobile, which the trial court had excluded from the probable cause determination on grounds that the reliability of the dog had not been demonstrated, the warrant that was issued to search the automobile lacked probable cause. The Washington Court of Appeals certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did probable cause exist to issue a warrant to search Neth’s automobile without the drug dog alerting police officers that drugs were present in the automobile?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for a unanimous Court vacated Neth’s conviction, ordered the evidence derived from the search suppressed, and remanded the case to the trial court, concluding that although Neth had acted nervously, had no identification, registration, or insurance documents, told police officers that a large quantity of cash was present in the automobile, possessed plastic bags of the sort frequently used to transport illegal drugs, and had previously been convicted of possession of heroin, these facts by themselves, although suspicious, were insufficient to establish probable cause to issue a warrant to search the automobile.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: NCF Fin., Inc. v. St. Paul Fire & Marine Ins. Co.
questions: Whether an additional insured is subject to a disappearance-inventory loss exclusion in an insurance contract and, if so, whether NCF Financial produced sufficient evidence of what happened to missing computer equipment to avoid summary judgment.

title: Griffin v. Thurston County
facts: In anticipation of constructing a home on a waterfront lot, petitioner Jeff Griffin submitted an application for an onsite sewage system to respondent Thurston County’s Board of Health, which was approved by a health officer. Upon appeal of the health officer’s decision by Griffin’s neighbors, the board reversed the health officer’s decision and rejected Griffin’s application, ruling that Griffin had not satisfied Thurston County Sanitary Code Article IV §21.4.5.3, which mandates that all of the code’s requirements be met in order for an onsite sewage system permit to be issued, insofar as the application relied upon waivers, setback adjustments, and other modifications of the rules to achieve compliance. Griffin subsequently sought review of the board’s decision in the Superior Court for Thurston County, which reversed the board and ordered the requested permit issued. Thurston County appealed the superior court’s decision to the Washington Court of Appeals, which reversed the superior court and reinstated the board’s decision. Griffin appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May an application for an onsite sewage system rely upon waivers, setback adjustments, and other modifications of the rules in order to satisfy all requirements for purposes of Thurston County Sanitary Code Article IV §21.4.5.3? If so, did Griffin’s application satisfy all requirements?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals on alternate grounds, concluding that although an application may rely upon waivers, setback adjustments, and other modifications of the rules to achieve compliance with all requirements, Griffin’s application did not achieve compliance in any event as it did not meet septic tank and water line requirements.

title: Tacoma Narrows Constructors v. Nippon Steel-Kawada Bridge, Inc.
questions: Whether Tacoma Narrows Bridge construction disputes should be sent to arbitration under International Chamber of Commerce arbitration rules or decided by a court?

title: In re personal restraint of Bonds
facts: Respondent Robert Bonds appealed his conviction in the Superior Court for Pierce County on charges of attempted murder and unlawful possession of a firearm by filing a personal restraint petition in the Washington Court of Appeals that asserted that the trial court had violated his right to confront witnesses against him by admitting into evidence out of court statements made by his co-defendants and that his attorney had been ineffective in raising the issue on appeal. After a delay of nearly a year, the Washington Court of Appeals ruled that Bonds’ petition was meritorious, referred the case to a panel of judges for a decision on the merits, and appointed counsel for Bonds. Bonds’ new attorney subsequently filed a motion to amend the personal restraint petition to add additional claims asserting that the trial court also violated Bonds’ right to a public trial and the public’s right to open court proceedings. Despite the fact that the one year statute of limitations for collateral attacks on convictions established by Washington Revised Code §10.73.090 had expired, the Washington Court of Appeals granted the motion, holding that the motion should be granted on equitable grounds given the fact that the delay in deciding whether Bonds’ petition was meritorious and in appointing counsel had consumed nearly the entire tolling period and left Bonds’ new attorney with no time to discover the public trial issues. After the Washington Court of Appeals subsequently decided the merits of the case and vacated Bonds’ convictions, the state of Washington appealed the decision to grant Bonds’ untimely motion to amend his personal restraint petition.
questions: Did the Washington Court of Appeals err in granting Bonds’ untimely motion to amend his personal restraint petition on equitable grounds?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and reinstated Bonds’ convictions, concluding that although the one year statute of limitations established by §10.73.090 may be waived at a court’s discretion on equitable grounds, these grounds are limited to instances in which a personal restraint petition is untimely due to bad faith, deception, or false assurances.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Arlington v. Central Puget Sound Growth Management Hearings Board
facts: After Snohomish County enacted an ordinance changing the designation and zoning of a parcel of land from agricultural to urban and general commercial, the petitioner Central Puget Sound Growth Management Hearings Board held a hearing to determine whether the redesignation complied with the Growth Management Act (Washington Revised Code §36.70A). The Board decided that the redesignation was not guided by and in substantial compliance with §36.70A and remanded the ordinance for legislative action to bring it into compliance. The respondent city of Arlington appealed the Board’s decision to the Superior Court for Snohomish County, which affirmed the decision. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, ruling that the redesignation was not clearly erroneous and that the Board had failed to consider important evidence in the record. The Board appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was the redesignation by Snohomish County of the contested parcel of land from agricultural to urban and general commercial clearly erroneous in light of the requirements of §36.70A?
conclusions: Justice Sanders’ opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, holding that although the Board had previously found that the original designation of the land as agricultural was not clearly erroneous, this does not necessarily render the subsequent redesignation of the land as urban and general commercial erroneous as the issues in the two cases were not identical and the Board failed to consider important evidence in the record indicating changed circumstances.

title: In re recall of Davis
facts: Respondent Christopher Clifford, a registered voter in the Port of Seattle jurisdiction, filed a petition to recall Port of Seattle Commissioner Pat Davis. A sufficiency hearing was subsequently held in the Superior Court for King County, which ruled that Clifford’s charges that Davis committed malfeasance by signing a memorandum obligating the Port of Seattle to pay an outgoing employee additional compensation not voted on or approved by the commissioners and by voting in executive session in violation of the Open Public Meetings Act (Washington Revised Code §42.30) were factually and legally sufficient for purposes of Washington Revised Code §29A.56.110, which governs recall petitions. Davis appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Are the charges detailed in the recall petition factually and legally sufficient?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed in part and reversed in part the superior court, concluding that the charge that Davis voted in executive session in violation of the Open Public Meetings Act was factually insufficient insofar as it was based upon information gathered from the media rather than upon personal knowledge. However, the Court also held that the charge that Davis obligated the Port of Seattle to pay an outgoing employee additional compensation not voted on or approved by the commissioners was both factually and legally sufficient insofar as the record contained the signed memorandum authorizing the compensation and the charged conduct represented serious malfeasance. Thus, the Court remanded the case to the superior court to prepare a ballot synopsis.

title: State of Washington v. Radcliffe
facts: Petitioner James Radcliffe was convicted of third degree rape and indecent liberties in the Superior Court for Thurston County after a trial in which Radcliffe’s confession to police following his arrest was admitted into evidence. Radcliffe appealed his conviction, asserting that although he initially waived his Miranda rights when apprised of them by the first officer that interrogated him, the confession should nonetheless have been suppressed insofar as the second officer that interrogated him and that recorded the confession subsequently continued interrogating him after he requested an attorney. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Radcliffe’s conviction. Radcliffe appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did Radcliffe’s request for an attorney after initially waiving his Miranda rights foreclose further questioning?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Radcliffe’s request for an attorney after initially waiving his Miranda rights was equivocal and that the officer interrogating Radcliffe was therefore not required to cease questioning. Thus, as Radcliffe’s subsequent confession was voluntary and made with knowledge of his rights, the Court held that it was properly admitted into evidence.

title: Residents Opposed to Kittitas Turbines v. State Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council
facts: In separate actions, petitioners Residents Opposed to Kittitas Turbines and Kittitas County sought judicial review of respondents State Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council and Governor Christine Gregoire’s final decision authorizing the preemption of Kittitas County laws to permit the construction and operation of wind turbines for energy production by Horizon Wind Energy, L.L.C. The petitioners alleged that the EFSEC could not preempt county laws regarding the siting of a wind powered energy facility, that EFSEC’s members violated the appearance of fairness doctrine, and that EFSEC’s decision to preempt Kittitas County laws, authorized by Governor Gregoire, was not supported by substantial evidence that Horizon did everything it could to comply with the county laws. EFSEC filed a motion to certify the petitions for review to the Supreme Court of Washington pursuant to Wash. Rev. Code §80.50.140. The Thurston County Superior Court certified the petitions, and the petitioners challenged the Supreme Court of Washington’s jurisdiction to review the petitions directly.
questions: Does the Supreme Court of Washington have jurisdiction to review a petition certified from Superior Court of the Governor’s decision to approve an energy facility site? Does the Governor have the authority to permit the construction and operation of wind turbines for energy production in the State without authorization from the county in which the turbines will be placed?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for a unanimous Court held that according to the Energy Facilities Site Locations Act (EFSLA), Wash. Rev. Code chapter §80.50, the Thurston County Superior Court had the discretion to determine if the petition met certain criteria for certification to the Court. Further, the certification procedures do not violate Art. IV of the State Constitution by vesting direct review in the Supreme Court of Washington without requiring initial review by the Superior Court. Thus, the EFSLA, specifically Wash. Rev. Code §80.50.140, appropriately confers appellate jurisdiction on the Supreme Court of Washington. As to the second issue, the Court affirmed the Governor’s final decision to approve the site certification application, holding that the Governor properly exercised her authority under EFSLA. Also, the petitioners failed to provide substantial evidence that Horizon had no interest in finding compromise with Kittitas County. Rather, substantial evidence supports that EFSEC properly applied the standards of preemption according to Washington Admin. Code 463-28-040, and did not violate its preemption powers, or the appearance of fairness doctrine.

title: State of Washington v. Gossage
facts: Petitioner Henry Gossage was convicted of four felony sex offenses and sentenced to a term of imprisonment to be followed by a term of community custody and to pay restitution. Following Gossage’s completion of his terms of imprisonment and community custody, he petitioned the Superior Court for King County for a certificate of discharge restoring his civil rights. The superior court rejected Gossage’s petition. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the superior court’s decision. Gossage appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is Gossage entitled to a certificate of discharge despite the fact that he has not paid all of the restitution he owes?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and remanded the case to the superior court for entry of an order granting a certificate of discharge, concluding that Gossage is entitled to a certificate of discharge despite the fact that he has not paid all of the restitution he owes insofar as legal financial obligations such as restitution orders expire ten years after the release of an offender from confinement under Washington Revised Code §9.94A.760(4) unless extended. Thus, as the restitution order was not extended and more than ten years has elapsed since Gossage’s release, Gossage has no remaining sentence requirements precluding him from receiving a certificate of discharge.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Cayenne
facts: Respondent Gerald Cayenne, a member of the Chehalis Indian Tribe and resident of the Chehalis Indian Reservation, was convicted of unlawful use of nets to take fish in the Superior Court for Grays Harbor County and prohibited from possessing gill nets as a condition of his sentence. Cayenne subsequently appealed the trial court’s order, asserting that the trial court exceeded its authority to impose a crime related prohibition insofar as the prohibition restricts his ability to fish while on the reservation. The Washington Court of Appeals partially reversed the trial court’s order, holding that while the trial court could prohibit Cayenne from possessing gill nets while off of the reservation, it could not prohibit Cayenne from possessing gill nets while on the reservation. The state of Washington appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does a state court have the authority to impose a crime related prohibition that regulates the activity of a tribal member on tribal land?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that as Cayenne committed the crime of unlawful use of nets while outside of the Chehalis Indian Reservation, the trial court had personal jurisdiction over him and therefore had the authority to impose crime related prohibitions regulating his activity on and off tribal land.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: In re disciplinary proceeding against Cramer
facts: Following a hearing before the Washington State Bar Association’s disciplinary board, Stephen Cramer was suspended from the practice of law for eight months and formally reprimanded for placing advance fee payments from a client in his personal business account rather than in a trust account in violation of Washington Rules of Professional Conduct §8.4(c) and making misrepresentations to the Washington State Bar Association regarding his handling of the funds in violation of Washington Rules of Professional Conduct §8.4(d). Cramer subsequently appealed the disciplinary board’s decision, claiming that it was not supported by a preponderance of the evidence as he had merely acted negligently.
questions: Was the disciplinary board’s finding that Cramer had been more than negligent in misplacing the funds and misrepresenting their disposition to the Washington State Bar Association supported by substantial evidence? If so, were the sanctions imposed upon Cramer appropriate given the balance of aggravating and mitigating factors?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the sanctions that had been imposed upon Cramer, concluding that although there was conflicting evidence regarding Cramer’s state of mind, the findings of the disciplinary board were supported by substantial evidence. The Court also held that the sanctions imposed were appropriate as the disciplinary board had properly found four aggravating factors (prior disciplinary offenses, substantial experience in the practice of law, multiple offenses, and refusal to acknowledge the wrongful nature of the conduct) and no mitigating factors.

title: State of Washington v. Roswell
facts: Petitioner Johnathon Roswell was charged with second degree child molestation and felony communication with a minor for immoral purposes. Roswell subsequently moved to stipulate to the existence of his prior convictions for sexual offenses in order to prevent the jury from being informed of them during the trial. The trial court rejected rejected Roswell’s motion, ruling that as a prior conviction for a sexual offense is an element of the crime of felony communication with a minor for immoral purposes insofar as communication with a minor for immoral purposes is a misdeameanor rather than a felony in cases in which the defendant has not previously been convicted of a sexual offense, allowing Roswell to stipulate to his prior convictions for sexual offenses would deny the state of Washington the ability to prove all elements of the charged crime to the jury. After Roswell was found guilty by the jury and sentenced, he appealed his conviction, asserting that evidence of prior convictions for sexual offenses is highly prejudicial propensity evidence and irrelevant. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Roswell’s conviction. Roswell appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the trial court err in rejecting Roswell’s motion to stipulate to his prior convictions for sexual offenses when these prior convictions constituted an element of the charged crime?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that despite the risk that a jury may conclude that a defendant has a propensity to commit the type of crime charged when evidence of prior convictions for the same type of crime is admitted, the trial court did not err in rejecting Roswell’s motion to stipulate to his prior convictions for sexual offenses as these convictions constituted elements of the charged crime that could not be bifurcated from the other elements.

title: In re personal restraint of Tobin
facts: Petitioner Douglas Tobin was convicted of unlawful possession of a firearm, theft, and numerous felony fish and wildlife violations in the Superior Court for Pierce County and sentenced to the statutory maximum of 116 months imprisonment for the unlawful possession of a firearm conviction and to 52 months imprisonment for the theft conviction. After the trial court erroneously entered the total sentence of 168 months as the sentence imposed for the unlawful possession of a firearm conviction on Tobin’s confinement order, Tobin filed a personal restraint petition in the Washington Court of Appeals that asserted that the trial court erred in including the felony fish and wildlife violations in calculating his offender score for the unlawful possession of a firearm conviction and that his sentence was facially invalid insofar as 168 months imprisonment exceeds the statutory maximum sentence for unlawful possession of a firearm. The Washington Court of Appeals dismissed Tobin’s petition, ruling that the trial court had properly included Tobin’s felony fish and wildlife violations in his offender score for the unlawful possession of a firearm conviction and that the error in documentation did not render his sentence facially invalid. Tobin appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the trial court err in including Tobin’s felony fish and wildlife violations in calculating his offender score for the unlawful possession of a firearm conviction? Is Tobin’s 168 month sentence for unlawful possession of a firearm facially invalid?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed in part and reversed in part the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Tobin’s felony fish and wildlife violations had been properly included in calculating his offender score for the unlawful possession of a firearm conviction insofar as these violations constitute Class C felonies and Washington Revised Code §9.94A.525(2)(a)-(c) requires the inclusion of all Class A, B, and C felonies in calculating offender scores. However, the Court also held that Tobin’s 168 month sentence for unlawful possession of a firearm is facially invalid as no court may impose a sentence in excess of that authorized by law. Thus, the Court remanded the case for resentencing to correct the error.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Washington v. Nguyen
facts: Petitioner Gabrielle Nguyen was convicted of possession of cocaine and physical control of a vehicle while under the influence of alcohol or drugs in the Superior Court for King County after police encountered her sitting behind the wheel of an automobile parked partially in the lane of travel while under the influence of stimulants and alcohol and a subsequent search of the automobile revealed cocaine. Nguyen subsequently appealed her conviction for physical control of a vehicle while under the influence of alcohol or drugs, asserting that as she had been found not guilty of driving while under the influence of alcohol or drugs she could not be convicted of the uncharged offense of physical control of a vehicle while under the influence of alcohol or drugs insofar as it is not an included offense of driving while under the influence of alcohol or drugs. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Nguyen’s conviction. Nguyen appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is physical control of a vehicle while under the influence of alcohol or drugs an included offense of driving while under the influence of alcohol or drugs?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed Nguyen’s conviction, concluding that although physical control of a vehicle while under the influence of alcohol or drugs is subject to the same penalties as driving while under the influence of alcohol or drugs, it is nonetheless an included offense of driving while under the influence of alcohol or drugs insofar as all of the elements of physical control of a vehicle while under the influence of alcohol or drugs are elements of driving while under the influence of alcohol or drugs and there is no requirement that an included offense have a lesser penalty than the charged offense.

title: Cornhusker Casualty Insurance Company v. Kachman
facts: In the course of hearing an appeal by Cornhusker Casualty Insurance Company asserting that Cornhusker Casualty Insurance Company had cancelled Chris Kachman’s insurance policy prior to an automobile accident involving one of Kachman’s employees that gave rise to the underlying litigation, the United States Court of Appeal for the Ninth Circuit certified to the Supreme Court of Washington the question of whether Cornhusker Casualty Insurance had given Kachman sufficient notice of cancellation under Washington Revised Code §48.18.290 by sending a letter via certified mail that was never received by Kachman.
questions: Did Cornhusker Casualty Insurance Company cancel Kachman’s insurance policy consistent with the requirements of §48.18.290 by sending a letter via certified mail that was never received?

title: In re disciplinary proceeding against Behrman
facts: Following a hearing before the respondent Washington State Bar Association’s disciplinary board, petitioner Bradley Behrman’s license to practice law was suspended for nine months and he was ordered to pay $500 in restitution and undergo counseling after the board found that he had violated several rules of professional conduct when he failed to collect a debt owed his client, failed to provide his client with sufficient information about the work he had performed and to resolve the resulting fee dispute, failed to respond to his client’s calls and emails and to provide his client her file upon request, removed disputed funds from a trust without his client’s knowledge or consent, and failed to cooperate with the disciplinary board’s investigation. Behrman subsequently appealed the disciplinary board’s sanction to the Supreme Court of Washington, asserting that the disciplinary board had erred in refusing to admit billing statements as evidence, erroneously concluded that he was not remorseful, erroneously found aggravating factors, and erroneously failed to find mitigating factors.
questions: Did the disciplinary board err in refusing to admit into evidence billing statements offered by Behrman? Was the disciplinary board’s conclusion that Behrman was not remorseful supported by substantial evidence? Did the disciplinary board properly weigh aggravating and mitigating factors in determining Behrman’s sanction?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court declined to overturn the disciplinary board’s sanction, concluding that the billing statements offered by Behrman were untimely and irrelevant and that substantial evidence supported the disciplinary board’s conclusion that Behrman was not remorseful given Behrman’s statements minimizing the consequences of his actions. The Court also held that the disciplinary board properly found that indifference to restitution constituted an aggravating factor and properly declined to find that personal and emotional problems constituted a mitigating factor and that the sanction imposed was proportional to the gravity of the violations.
